figures.name: Antony the Great
figures.dates: c. 251 to 356 (the Life says he died about 105 years old)
figures.places: Coma in Middle Egypt; the tombs near his village; a ruined fort at Pispir on the Nile (the "outer mountain"); the "inner mountain" near the Red Sea (Mount Colzim, where the Monastery of St Antony now stands); visits to Alexandria
figures.role: Egyptian farmer's son turned hermit; the most famous early desert monk and a model for the whole monastic movement; ally of Athanasius against the Arians
figures.status_note: Saint in every ancient church: Catholic and Anglican (17 January), Eastern Orthodox (17 January), Coptic Orthodox (22 Tobi, about 30 January). Cautions: almost everything we know comes from Athanasius's Life, written soon after his death by a bishop with an agenda. It stresses that Antony was unlettered, obedient to bishops and fiercely anti-Arian, and it is full of demons and miracles. Seven Coptic letters under his name are accepted as genuine by many scholars (Samuel Rubenson, 1995); they show a more learned man who used Platonic and Origen-like ideas about the mind. No pre-1929 English of the letters was found, so they are not used here. Jerome's Life of Paul the Hermit, where Antony meets Paul, is largely legend.
figures.hook: At eighteen he heard one Gospel verse read in church, walked out, gave away three hundred acres of farmland, and spent the next eighty-odd years in the desert, where emperors wrote to him and he hardly bothered to reply.

stories.story: After his parents died he walked into church as Matthew 19:21 was read ("go and sell that you have and give to the poor"). He went straight out and gave the family land, three hundred acres, to the villagers. He sold the rest, kept a little for his young sister, and later placed her with a community of virgins.
stories.source: Athanasius, Life of Antony 2-3

stories.story: He shut himself in a deserted fort for nearly twenty years, fed with bread lowered twice a year. When friends finally broke the door down, he walked out neither fat nor thin, "the same as they had known him before".
stories.source: Athanasius, Life of Antony 12-14

stories.story: During the persecution under Maximinus (311) the governor ordered all monks out of Alexandria. Everyone else hid. Antony washed his garment and stood all the next day on a raised place in front of the governor. He wanted martyrdom but would not hand himself in, so he spent the persecution nursing confessors in the mines and prisons.
stories.source: Athanasius, Life of Antony 46

stories.story: Greek philosophers came to mock him for being unable to read. He asked them which came first, mind or letters. They said mind. "Whoever, therefore, has a sound mind has not need of letters," he answered, and they left amazed.
stories.source: Athanasius, Life of Antony 73

stories.story: A hunter was shocked to find Antony relaxing and enjoying himself with the monks. Antony told him to draw his bow, then draw it further, then further still. The hunter said it would break. "So it is in the work of God," Antony said: stretch the brothers too far and they break, so let them off the strictness now and then.
stories.source: Verba Seniorum (Pelagius) 10.2, PL 73; own summary from the Latin

stories.story: He was twice sent word that ordinary people in the city had outdone him. One was a tailor in Alexandria who simply thanked God morning and night and thought himself the worst man in town. Antony told him, "I, who have passed the whole of my life in the desert, separated [from men], have never overtaken thee."
stories.source: Budge, The Paradise vol. 2, Questions and Answers on the Rule of Life, nos. 2-3

stories.story: The blind scholar Didymus admitted that his blindness grieved him. Antony told him a wise man should not mourn eyes that ants, flies and gnats also have, but rejoice in the inner sight given to saints and apostles.
stories.source: Jerome, Letter 68.2 (Jerome says it happened in his childhood); also Socrates, Church History 4.25 ("it is said")

stories.story: Dying, he ordered his two companions to bury him secretly so that no one would keep his body in a house as Egyptians did with holy men. He left one sheepskin to Athanasius and one to Bishop Serapion. His grave was unknown.
stories.source: Athanasius, Life of Antony 90-92

stories.story: Decades later, in Milan, a visitor told Augustine about Antony. Hearing that Antony had been converted by one Gospel verse read aloud, Augustine went back to the garden, opened Paul's letters at random, and was converted himself.
stories.source: Augustine, Confessions 8.6 and 8.12

stories.story: Jerome's legend: at about ninety Antony learned that an older hermit, Paul, lived deeper in the desert, walked to find him, and came back saying he had seen Paul in Paradise. Treat as legend.
stories.source: Jerome, Life of Paul the First Hermit 13

temperament.evidence: His biographer says strangers could pick him out of a crowd of monks by his face: "he was never downcast, for his mind was joyous."
temperament.source: Athanasius, Life of Antony 67

temperament.evidence: Coming out after twenty years alone, his soul was "neither contracted as if by grief, nor relaxed by pleasure, nor possessed by laughter or dejection".
temperament.source: Athanasius, Life of Antony 14

temperament.evidence: He met sneering philosophers through an interpreter, turned their questions back on them, and "Antony smiled" when they were stuck.
temperament.source: Athanasius, Life of Antony 72-77

temperament.evidence: He "was not ashamed to bow his head to bishops and presbyters" and would ask questions and learn from anyone.
temperament.source: Athanasius, Life of Antony 67

temperament.evidence: He drove Arian visitors off his mountain, "saying that their words were worse than the poison of serpents."
temperament.source: Athanasius, Life of Antony 68

temperament.evidence: When a possessed young man shoved him, and his companions were angry, he said: "Be not angry with the young man, for it is not he, but the demon which is in him."
temperament.source: Athanasius, Life of Antony 64

temperament.evidence: He hated being dragged down from the mountain, but went when judges sent prisoners to beg his help.
temperament.source: Athanasius, Life of Antony 84

genuine_lines.work: Athanasius, Life of Antony
genuine_lines.translation: H. Ellershaw, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, vol. 4 (1892), as revised for New Advent

misattributed.line: The Philokalia's opening work, "On the Character of Men and on the Virtuous Life: 170 Texts", printed under the name of St Antony the Great
misattributed.truth: Not by Antony. It is a Stoic and Platonist collection; the modern English Philokalia translators (Palmer, Sherrard and Ware, 1979) say it cannot be his. Status: secondary knowledge, not re-read here.

misattributed.line: Prayers to find lost things ("Saint Anthony, please come around...")
misattributed.truth: These belong to Anthony of Padua (died 1231), a Franciscan, not to Antony of Egypt. The two are often mixed up online.

misattributed.line: The pig, the bell and the T-shaped cross shown with him in Western art
misattributed.truth: These come from the medieval Hospital Brothers of St Antony (the Antonines), who kept pigs and cared for victims of "St Anthony's fire", not from anything in his Life. Secondary knowledge.

misattributed.line: "I saw the snares of the enemy... and a voice said: Humility"
misattributed.truth: Genuine, but versions differ: in the Greek sayings a voice answers him; in Budge's Syriac the devils themselves say it. Quote a named translation.

opinions.position: Give possessions away. Wanting to own things is pointless because you cannot take them with you; take virtues instead.
opinions.side_note: Wealth: firmly on the side of renouncing it, not merely using it well.
opinions.quote: Therefore let the desire of possession take hold of no one, for what gain is it to acquire these things which we cannot take with us?
opinions.work: Athanasius, Life of Antony
opinions.translation: H. Ellershaw, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, vol. 4 (1892), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split. Most people, Christians included, think it is fine to own things if you are generous. A minority admire radical giving. Few would sell everything.

opinions.position: Half-renunciation causes trouble. Someone who leaves the world but keeps part of his money gets torn apart by it.
opinions.side_note: Wealth: against keeping a safety net.
opinions.quote: Even thus are those who wish to go out from the world, and who nevertheless leave themselves certain possessions, wherefrom arise for their owners war and strife.
opinions.work: Sayings of the Desert Fathers (Syriac collection, in Budge, The Paradise, vol. 2)
opinions.location: Book I, chapter 5, no. 178 (he made the man carry raw meat through a village so dogs and birds tore at him)
opinions.translation: E. A. Wallis Budge, The Paradise or Garden of the Holy Fathers, vol. 2 (1907), from the Syriac collection of ʿAnan-Isho; Wikisource transcription
opinions.today: Most people today would say keeping savings is simple prudence. Strongly one-sided against Antony.

opinions.position: Book learning is not needed for wisdom or faith. A sound mind comes first; letters are its invention.
opinions.side_note: Learning: on the side that schooling is unnecessary for knowing God. (Caution: his own letters suggest he was more educated than this picture.)
opinions.quote: Whoever, therefore, has a sound mind has not need of letters.
opinions.work: Athanasius, Life of Antony
opinions.translation: H. Ellershaw, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, vol. 4 (1892), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split. Many admire self-taught common sense; many others think serious faith needs study. Good quiz material.

opinions.position: Faith is stronger than argument. Those who have faith do not need proofs, and proofs often cannot express what faith knows.
opinions.side_note: Learning or questioning: on the side of faith over reasoned proof.
opinions.quote: Wherefore to those who have the inworking through faith, demonstrative argument is needless, or even superfluous.
opinions.work: Athanasius, Life of Antony
opinions.translation: H. Ellershaw, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, vol. 4 (1892), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split. Apologetics fans and sceptics want arguments; many believers say faith does not need them.

opinions.position: Nature itself is a book in which God can be read, any time.
opinions.side_note: Creation: strongly positive about reading God in the natural world.
opinions.quote: My book, O philosopher,' replied Anthony, 'is the nature of things that are made, and it is present whenever I wish to read the words of God.
opinions.work: Socrates Scholasticus, Church History
opinions.translation: A. C. Zenos, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, vol. 2 (1890), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Most people agree they feel close to God in nature. Fairly one-sided today, so weak as a sorting question on its own.

opinions.position: You do not need to travel to become good. Virtue is already inside you; the Greeks cross the sea for knowledge, but the kingdom of heaven is within.
opinions.side_note: Pilgrimage: against travelling for holiness.
opinions.quote: That they may get knowledge, the Greeks live abroad and cross the sea, but we have no need to depart from home for the sake of the kingdom of heaven, nor to cross the sea for the sake of virtue.
opinions.work: Athanasius, Life of Antony
opinions.translation: H. Ellershaw, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, vol. 4 (1892), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split. Many Catholics and Orthodox value pilgrimage; many Protestants and secular people say God or goodness is found at home.

opinions.position: Goodness is natural and within reach. It needs only your willingness, because the soul was made good.
opinions.side_note: Grace and effort: optimistic about the will (though the Life also credits every victory to Christ, chapter 5).
opinions.quote: Wherefore virtue has need at our hands of willingness alone, since it is in us and is formed from us.
opinions.work: Athanasius, Life of Antony
opinions.translation: H. Ellershaw, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, vol. 4 (1892), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split. Many people say being good is mostly a choice; many Christians say we cannot be good without grace.

opinions.position: A monk belongs away from people. Staying long among them drains him, like a fish on dry land.
opinions.side_note: Solitude: strongly for withdrawal (though he did come out to help).
opinions.quote: Fishes, if they remain long on dry land, die. And so monks lose their strength if they loiter among you and spend their time with you.
opinions.work: Athanasius, Life of Antony
opinions.translation: H. Ellershaw, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, vol. 4 (1892), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Most people today prize community and fear isolation. Introverts and people drawn to retreats would side with him.

opinions.position: But ordinary life in the city can be holier than a lifetime in the desert. God showed him a tailor and a doctor in town who had outdone him.
opinions.side_note: Solitude or family-calling: on the side that ordinary working life can equal the desert.
opinions.quote: Verily, as the man who worketh in gold, and who doeth beautiful work, cleanly, and in peace, even so art thou; through thy beautiful thoughts thou wilt inherit the kingdom of God
opinions.work: Sayings of the Desert Fathers (Syriac collection, in Budge, The Paradise, vol. 2)
opinions.location: Book II, Questions and Answers on the Rule of Life, no. 2
opinions.translation: E. A. Wallis Budge, The Paradise or Garden of the Holy Fathers, vol. 2 (1907), from the Syriac collection of ʿAnan-Isho; Wikisource transcription
opinions.today: Almost everyone today agrees with this. One-sided, but it makes Antony surprising.

opinions.position: Strictness must be relaxed now and then. People stretched too far break like a bow.
opinions.side_note: Enjoyment: on the side that relaxing and enjoying company is right.
opinions.quote: “If I draw it beyond measure, the bow will break.” Abba Antony said to him: “So it is in the work of God. If we stretch the brothers beyond measure, they soon give way. So it is good to relax their strictness now and then.”
opinions.original_latin: Dixit ei venator: Si supra mensuram traxe­ ro, frangetur arcus. Dicit ei abbas Antonius: Ita est et in opere Dei: si plus a mensura tendimus, fratres cito deficiunt; expedit ergo una et una relaxare rigo­ rem eorum.
opinions.work: Verba Seniorum (Latin systematic Sayings of the Desert Fathers, tr. Pelagius the Deacon, 6th century)
opinions.translation: Own close rendering from the Latin Verba Seniorum of Pelagius the Deacon (Vitae Patrum book 5, PL 73), OCR text from Open Greek and Latin
opinions.today: Most people agree today. One-sided, but a striking contrast with his own harsh routine.

opinions.position: Harsh self-denial without good sense takes people away from God.
opinions.side_note: Asceticism: for discipline, against discipline without discernment.
opinions.quote: There are some monks who vex their bodies with the labours of abstinence and self-denial, and who, because they have not found understanding, are remote from the path of God.
opinions.work: Sayings of the Desert Fathers (Syriac collection, in Budge, The Paradise, vol. 2)
opinions.translation: E. A. Wallis Budge, The Paradise or Garden of the Holy Fathers, vol. 2 (1907), from the Syriac collection of ʿAnan-Isho; Wikisource transcription
opinions.today: Most people agree that extremes are unhealthy. Among the Fathers there is more of a split (compare Jerome or Simeon Stylites).

opinions.topic: new: the body and its needs
opinions.position: Eating and sleeping are embarrassing necessities. He ate alone so as not to be seen, gave the body a little time, and gave the rest to the soul.
opinions.side_note: Related to asceticism: a low view of bodily needs.
opinions.quote: And he used to eat and sleep, and go about all other bodily necessities with shame when he thought of the spiritual faculties of the soul.
opinions.work: Athanasius, Life of Antony
opinions.translation: H. Ellershaw, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, vol. 4 (1892), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Most people today would find this unhealthy. Strongly one-sided against him, but vivid as a sparring point.

opinions.position: He never washed his feet or bathed, and kept a hair shirt on to the end.
opinions.side_note: Asceticism: extreme in practice.
opinions.quote: And he neither bathed his body with water to free himself from filth, nor did he ever wash his feet, nor even endure so much as to put them into water, unless compelled by necessity.
opinions.work: Athanasius, Life of Antony
opinions.translation: H. Ellershaw, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, vol. 4 (1892), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Almost no one today would copy this. Use only as a story, not a statement.

opinions.topic: new: keeping a written record of your faults
opinions.position: Each day, write down what you did and what stirred in your soul, as if you would have to show it to others. The shame of being seen keeps you from sin.
opinions.side_note: A daily written self-examination.
opinions.quote: Let us each one note and write down our actions and the impulses of our soul as though we were going to relate them to each other.
opinions.work: Athanasius, Life of Antony
opinions.translation: H. Ellershaw, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, vol. 4 (1892), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split. Journalling is popular, but many would say shame is a bad motive. Good quiz material.

opinions.position: Never let the sun go down on anger, or on any other sin. Check yourself every day and deal with it before night.
opinions.side_note: Anger: on the side of settling it the same day.
opinions.quote: And especially he counselled them to meditate continually on the apostle's word, 'Let not the sun go down upon your wrath
opinions.work: Athanasius, Life of Antony
opinions.translation: H. Ellershaw, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, vol. 4 (1892), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Most people agree in principle. Fairly one-sided.

opinions.position: Do not condemn others. We often do wrong without knowing it, so leave judgment to God and feel for one another.
opinions.side_note: Correction: gentle, against condemning.
opinions.quote: Wherefore committing the judgment to Him, let us have sympathy one with another.
opinions.work: Athanasius, Life of Antony
opinions.translation: H. Ellershaw, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, vol. 4 (1892), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Most agree in principle; many practise the opposite.

opinions.topic: new: fear of God or love of God
opinions.position: He had moved beyond fear of God to love of Him.
opinions.side_note: Love, not fear, as the root of faith.
opinions.quote: I do not fear God, on the contrary I love Him.
opinions.work: Sayings of the Desert Fathers (Syriac collection, in Budge, The Paradise, vol. 2)
opinions.location: Book II, Questions and Answers on the Rule of Life
opinions.translation: E. A. Wallis Budge, The Paradise or Garden of the Holy Fathers, vol. 2 (1907), from the Syriac collection of ʿAnan-Isho; Wikisource transcription
opinions.today: Split. Many Christians say "the fear of the Lord" is essential; many others say God should never be feared. Good quiz material.

opinions.position: Miracles are Christ's work, not ours. Do not boast of healing or casting out demons, and do not rate a wonder-worker above someone who does none.
opinions.side_note: Signs: believes in them but plays them down.
opinions.quote: For the working of signs is not ours but the Saviour's work
opinions.work: Athanasius, Life of Antony
opinions.translation: H. Ellershaw, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, vol. 4 (1892), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split. Charismatic Christians prize signs; many others doubt them. His "play them down" stance is a middle position.

opinions.topic: new: wanting to know the future
opinions.position: Do not pray to know the future or treat foreknowledge as a reward. What matters is whether you kept the faith and the commandments.
opinions.side_note: Against curiosity about the future, including through spiritual gifts.
opinions.quote: And we neither ought to pray to know the future, nor to ask for it as the reward of our discipline
opinions.work: Athanasius, Life of Antony
opinions.translation: H. Ellershaw, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, vol. 4 (1892), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split. Horoscopes, prophecy conferences and prediction apps are popular. Many others agree with him.

opinions.position: Do not demand to know why God lets children die, the good be poor, or the wicked prosper. Look after your own soul.
opinions.side_note: Questioning: on the side of not pressing God for reasons about suffering.
opinions.quote: Anthony, take care of thine own self, for these matters are the judgements of God.
opinions.work: Sayings of the Desert Fathers (Syriac collection, in Budge, The Paradise, vol. 2)
opinions.location: Book II, Questions and Answers on the Rule of Life, no. 218 (a voice answering his question)
opinions.translation: E. A. Wallis Budge, The Paradise or Garden of the Holy Fathers, vol. 2 (1907), from the Syriac collection of ʿAnan-Isho; Wikisource transcription
opinions.today: Strongly split. Many people today think asking "why?" is honest and right; others accept mystery.

opinions.position: Saying "I do not know" about a hard passage of Scripture is the right answer, not a failure.
opinions.side_note: Scripture-sense or questioning: humble about interpretation.
opinions.quote: In truth, Abbâ Joseph, thou hast found the way to say, ‘I do not know.’
opinions.work: Sayings of the Desert Fathers (Syriac collection, in Budge, The Paradise, vol. 2)
opinions.translation: E. A. Wallis Budge, The Paradise or Garden of the Holy Fathers, vol. 2 (1907), from the Syriac collection of ʿAnan-Isho; Wikisource transcription
opinions.today: Most agree in principle. Many preachers and online debaters act otherwise.

opinions.topic: new: others' salvation is bound up with ours
opinions.position: You cannot be good in private. Your life or death depends on how you treat your neighbour.
opinions.side_note: Community over private piety.
opinions.quote: A man’s life or death cometh from his neighbour; if we benefit our brother we benefit ourselves, and if we offend him we sin against God.
opinions.work: Sayings of the Desert Fathers (Syriac collection, in Budge, The Paradise, vol. 2)
opinions.location: Book II, Questions and Answers on the Rule of Life, no. 33
opinions.translation: E. A. Wallis Budge, The Paradise or Garden of the Holy Fathers, vol. 2 (1907), from the Syriac collection of ʿAnan-Isho; Wikisource transcription
opinions.today: Most agree. Fairly one-sided.

opinions.position: In persecution, do not hand yourself in, but do not hide either. He stood openly before the governor and served prisoners.
opinions.side_note: Flight: neither flight nor volunteering for death.
opinions.quote: And he longed to suffer martyrdom, but not being willing to give himself up, he ministered to the confessors in the mines and in the prisons.
opinions.work: Athanasius, Life of Antony
opinions.translation: H. Ellershaw, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, vol. 4 (1892), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Hard to poll today. Most would say avoid death if you can while helping others. His middle path is attractive.

opinions.position: Emperors are only men. He was reluctant even to answer their letters; when he did, he told them to care for justice and the poor and remember judgment.
opinions.side_note: State and religion: respectful of Christian emperors but unimpressed by power.
opinions.quote: Do not be astonished if an emperor writes to us, for he is a man; but rather wonder that God wrote the Law for men and has spoken to us
opinions.work: Athanasius, Life of Antony
opinions.translation: H. Ellershaw, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, vol. 4 (1892), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Most people today agree rulers are only human. His refusal to be flattered by power is admired widely.

opinions.topic: new: keeping away from people with wrong beliefs
opinions.position: Have no fellowship with schismatics or heretics. He would talk to them only to urge them to change.
opinions.side_note: A hard line on religious separation.
opinions.quote: Have no fellowship with the schismatics, nor any dealings at all with the heretical Arians.
opinions.work: Athanasius, Life of Antony
opinions.translation: H. Ellershaw, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, vol. 4 (1892), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Strongly split. Most people today favour friendship across beliefs; some Christians still separate. Compare Poemen, who fed heretics.

opinions.topic: new: relics and the bodies of the dead
opinions.position: Bury the dead, even saints. Keeping holy bodies unburied at home is wrong; Christ's own body was laid in a tomb. He ordered his own grave hidden.
opinions.side_note: Against the Egyptian custom of keeping holy bodies in houses (his Latin editor Rosweyde notes he was not against relics as such).
opinions.quote: For the bodies of the patriarchs and prophets are until now preserved in tombs, and the very body of the Lord was laid in a tomb
opinions.work: Athanasius, Life of Antony
opinions.translation: H. Ellershaw, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, vol. 4 (1892), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split. Catholic and Orthodox Christians venerate relics; many Protestants and secular people find displays of bodies odd. Handle carefully: he opposed a custom, not relics in general.

opinions.topic: new: thinking about your own death every day
opinions.position: Wake each morning as if you will not live to evening, and lie down as if you will not wake. Then you will not sin, hoard or hold grudges.
opinions.side_note: A daily practice of remembering death.
opinions.quote: For if we too live as though dying daily, we shall not sin.
opinions.work: Athanasius, Life of Antony
opinions.translation: H. Ellershaw, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, vol. 4 (1892), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split. "Memento mori" is popular again, but many find thinking about death every day morbid. Good quiz material.

opinions.position: Do not mourn a lost bodily faculty. He told the blind Didymus that eyes are shared with gnats and flies, and inner sight is the gift that matters.
opinions.side_note: Grief: firm, even brusque, toward loss.
opinions.quote: I am surprised that a wise man should grieve at the loss of a faculty which he shares with ants and flies and gnats, and not rejoice rather in having one of which only saints and apostles have been thought worthy.
opinions.work: Jerome, Letter 68 to Castrutius
opinions.location: Letter 68, section 2 (Jerome reporting a conversation he dates to his childhood)
opinions.translation: W. H. Fremantle, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, vol. 6 (1893), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Many today would find this unkind to disabled people; others find it freeing. Split, but handle with care.

opinions.position: He started with the full command ("turn the other cheek") and kept lowering the bar for visitors who said they could not. When they refused even the least, he said they needed prayer.
opinions.side_note: Humour and realism about forgiveness.
opinions.quote: If ye cannot turn the other cheek, continue [to be smitten] on the one cheek
opinions.work: Sayings of the Desert Fathers (Syriac collection, in Budge, The Paradise, vol. 2)
opinions.translation: E. A. Wallis Budge, The Paradise or Garden of the Holy Fathers, vol. 2 (1907), from the Syriac collection of ʿAnan-Isho; Wikisource transcription
opinions.today: Split. Many Christians think turning the other cheek is an ideal few can live; others treat it as a plain command.

opinions.topic: new: working for your own bread
opinions.position: Work with your hands for your food and give part to the needy. In the desert he grew his own grain so as not to burden the monks who brought him bread.
opinions.side_note: Self-support over dependence.
opinions.quote: He worked, however, with his hands, having heard, 'he who is idle let him not eat
opinions.work: Athanasius, Life of Antony
opinions.translation: H. Ellershaw, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, vol. 4 (1892), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Most agree. Fairly one-sided today.

sparring.over: Whether the Son of God is a created being. He came down to Alexandria to denounce them as "the forerunner of Antichrist", drove Arian visitors off his mountain, and told his monks on his deathbed to have nothing to do with them.
The Meletian split in the Egyptian church; he never held communion with them.
Antony wrote again and again asking him to disbelieve the Meletians and recall the exiled Athanasius. Constantine refused and told him not to overlook the decision of a synod of bishops.

sparring.with: Balacius, an Arian general in Egypt
sparring.over: Balacius beat virgins and flogged monks. Antony wrote warning that wrath was coming; Balacius spat on the letter and died days later after a horse bite. (Athanasius's account.)
The custom of keeping holy people's bodies unburied at home. He urged bishops to forbid it and rebuked the laity.
Ammon complained that he worked harder than Antony and yet Antony was more famous. Antony: "Because I also love the Lord more than thou."
sparring.source: Budge, The Paradise vol. 2, Questions and Answers on the Rule of Life, no. 180

figures.name: Amma Syncletica
figures.dates: c. 4th century (often given as c. 320 to 400; she died about 80)
figures.places: Born in Alexandria to a family from Macedonia; lived as an ascetic outside the city
figures.role: Desert Mother and teacher of women ascetics; the most quoted woman in the Sayings of the Desert Fathers
figures.status_note: Saint in the Catholic Church (5 January) and the Eastern Orthodox Church (4 or 5 January). Cautions: everything comes from one Greek Life, once credited to Athanasius but written later (Baring-Gould already called the attribution unfounded; scholars date it to the 5th century), and from sayings in the Apophthegmata drawn from that Life. The facts of her life cannot be checked. No public-domain English translation of the Life exists; the lines below are own renderings from the 6th-century Latin of Pelagius, plus Baring-Gould's loose 1872 English. The Latin text used is uncorrected OCR (one word, "mater" for "mutes", is an OCR slip).
figures.hook: A rich, beautiful Alexandrian heiress who cut off her hair to scare off suitors, gave everything away to care for her blind sister, and ended as the desert's sharpest voice against extreme fasting.

stories.story: Born in Alexandria to wealthy parents from Macedonia, she refused every suitor. After her parents died she cared for her blind sister, cut off her hair and sold her estates.
stories.source: Baring-Gould, Lives of the Saints, 5 January (summarising the Greek Life)

stories.story: She tried to live hidden, but young women found her and asked for teaching. She did not want the role and took it anyway.
stories.source: Baring-Gould, Lives of the Saints, 5 January

stories.story: She died about eighty after three years of cancer of the mouth and lung disease. The tumour so disfigured her face and smelled so badly that she finally let it be treated with embalming mixture, to protect the women nursing her.
stories.source: Baring-Gould, Lives of the Saints, 5 January

temperament.evidence: Baring-Gould, who read her Life, says "her words abound in practical common sense."
temperament.source: Baring-Gould, Lives of the Saints, 5 January

temperament.evidence: She wanted to stay hidden and was pushed into teaching by the women who came to her.
temperament.source: Baring-Gould, Lives of the Saints, 5 January

temperament.evidence: Her best-known teaching is that the devil's kind of fasting is recognised by its lack of measure.
temperament.source: Verba Seniorum 10.72

temperament.evidence: She bore three years of a disfiguring cancer, according to her Life.
temperament.source: Baring-Gould, Lives of the Saints, 5 January

genuine_lines.quote: Just as a ship cannot be built without nails, so no one can be saved without humility.
genuine_lines.original_latin: Dixit beatæ memoriae Syncletica : Sicut impos­ sibile est navim fabricari sine acutis, ita impossi­ bile est hominem sine humilitate salvari.
genuine_lines.work: Verba Seniorum (Latin systematic Sayings of the Desert Fathers, tr. Pelagius the Deacon, 6th century)

genuine_lines.quote: There is a grief that is useful, and there is a grief that destroys.
genuine_lines.original_latin: Est tristitia utilis, et est tristi­ tia quae corrumpit.

genuine_lines.original_latin: Sicut thesaurus ma-, nifestus cito expenditur, ita et virtus quaelibet, cum innotuerit vel publicata fuerit, exterminabitur (Ruff., I. III, n. 114). Sicut enim cera solvitur a facie ignis, ita et anima laudibus inanitur; et amittit virtutum rigorem.

genuine_lines.original_latin: Semper enim quod sine mensura est, corruptibile est.

genuine_lines.quote: There is an asceticism which is of the devil. How are we to distinguish right asceticism from that which is wrong? By its moderation.
genuine_lines.work: Baring-Gould, Lives of the Saints (free rendering of the Greek Life of Syncletica)
genuine_lines.translation: S. Baring-Gould, The Lives of the Saints, vol. 1 (1872), his own free rendering of the Greek Life of Syncletica; Project Gutenberg

genuine_lines.quote: we all know how we can be saved, but we fail through our own carelessness.

misattributed.line: No false lines attributed to her were found in this search.
misattributed.truth: Her risk is different: modern books quote her from copyrighted translations (Benedicta Ward 1975, Bongie, Castelli), and many online versions are paraphrases of those. Use the Latin or Greek and render afresh.

opinions.position: Fasting and self-denial must have measure. Crash fasts followed by feasting please the devil; extremes corrupt.
opinions.side_note: Asceticism: firmly for moderation within discipline.
opinions.quote: Do you suddenly fast four or five days on end, and then undo your strength with a heap of food? That delights the devil. Whatever is without measure always corrupts.
opinions.original_latin: Non subito quatuor aut quinque dies continuos jejunas, et iterum mul­ titudine ciborum solvis virtutem ? hoc enim laetifi­ cat diabolum. Semper enim quod sine mensura est, corruptibile est.
opinions.work: Verba Seniorum (Latin systematic Sayings of the Desert Fathers, tr. Pelagius the Deacon, 6th century)
opinions.translation: Own close rendering from the Latin Verba Seniorum of Pelagius the Deacon (Vitae Patrum book 5, PL 73), OCR text from Open Greek and Latin
opinions.today: Most people agree with moderation. The more telling split is with Fathers like Antony who practised extreme fasts.

opinions.position: Do not use health as an excuse to skip a fast. People who do not fast get sick just as often.
opinions.side_note: Asceticism: firm, not soft. She is moderate, not lax.
opinions.quote: Have you begun fasting? Don't make pretexts to wriggle out of it on the score of health, for the lady who does not fast is just as much subject to maladies as she who does.
opinions.work: Baring-Gould, Lives of the Saints (free rendering of the Greek Life of Syncletica)
opinions.translation: S. Baring-Gould, The Lives of the Saints, vol. 1 (1872), his own free rendering of the Greek Life of Syncletica; Project Gutenberg
opinions.today: Split. Many people today think health comes first and fasting is optional; others enjoy her bluntness.

opinions.position: Obedience is better than your own heroic self-denial, because self-denial breeds pride and obedience breeds humility.
opinions.side_note: Choosing obedience over personal achievement.
opinions.quote: Living in community, we put obedience ahead of any self-denial. Self-denial carries pride with it; obedience promises the humility that fits us.
opinions.original_latin: Quia in congregatione r manentes cuilibet continentiae obedientiam. magis praeponimus ; quoniam continentia arrogantiam ha­ bet, obedieotia autem humilitatem congruam polli­ cetur.
opinions.work: Verba Seniorum (Latin systematic Sayings of the Desert Fathers, tr. Pelagius the Deacon, 6th century)
opinions.translation: Own close rendering from the Latin Verba Seniorum of Pelagius the Deacon (Vitae Patrum book 5, PL 73), OCR text from Open Greek and Latin
opinions.today: Strongly split. Most modern people distrust obedience and admire self-direction. Good quiz material.

opinions.position: Some sadness is good: grieving over your sins and over other people's blindness. Other sadness is aimless and comes from the enemy; drive it out with prayer and psalms.
opinions.side_note: Grief and emotions: sorts grief into healthy and harmful.
opinions.quote: There is a grief that is useful, and there is a grief that destroys. Useful grief is to groan for our sins and for our neighbours' ignorance, so that we do not fall from our purpose. But the enemy also sends a grief with no reason at all, which they call listlessness. Drive that spirit out, mostly by prayer and psalm-singing.
opinions.original_latin: Est tristitia utilis, et est tristi­ tia quae corrumpit. Tristitia ergo utilis est, ut pro peccatis ingemiscamus, et pro ignorantia proximo­ rum, et ut non cadamus a proposito, ut perfectio­ nem bonitatis attingamus: hae sunt species verae tri­ stitiae. Est enim et adversarii nostri ad haec quaedam conjunctio. Immittit enim tristitiam sine aliqua ra­ tione, quam taedium appellaverunt. Oportet ergo talem spiritum saepius orando et psallendo magis de­ pellere.
opinions.work: Verba Seniorum (Latin systematic Sayings of the Desert Fathers, tr. Pelagius the Deacon, 6th century)
opinions.translation: Own close rendering from the Latin Verba Seniorum of Pelagius the Deacon (Vitae Patrum book 5, PL 73), OCR text from Open Greek and Latin
opinions.today: Most people accept that some sadness is healthy. Treating low mood as spiritual attack is split, and touchy around depression.

opinions.position: Owning nothing is a great good, but only for those who can bear it. It is hard on the body and restful for the soul.
opinions.side_note: Wealth: for voluntary poverty, but not as a rule for everyone.
opinions.quote: She was asked whether owning nothing is the perfect good. She said: “It is a very great good for those who are able. Those who can bear it have hardship in the flesh, but rest in the soul.”
opinions.original_latin: Interrogata est beatae memoriae Syncletica: Si perfectum bonum est nihil habere ? Et illa dixit: Valde bonum est his qui possunt. Etenim hi qui to­ lerare possunt, tribulationem quidem carnis habent, sed animae requiem possident.
opinions.work: Verba Seniorum (Latin systematic Sayings of the Desert Fathers, tr. Pelagius the Deacon, 6th century)
opinions.location: book 5, 6.13 (That a monk should own nothing)
opinions.translation: Own close rendering from the Latin Verba Seniorum of Pelagius the Deacon (Vitae Patrum book 5, PL 73), OCR text from Open Greek and Latin
opinions.today: Split. Most people would not choose poverty; many admire simple living. Her "for those who can" is a moderate middle.

opinions.position: Greed is never satisfied. Traders who risk the sea for money always want more; believers should be as keen for God as they are for gain.
opinions.side_note: Wealth: critical of the endless chase for more.
opinions.quote: Those who gather riches through labour and the dangers of the sea want more the more they gain. They count what they have as nothing and strain after what they do not yet have. But we, who have none of the things worth seeking, will not even gain what is needed for the fear of God.
opinions.original_latin: Qui sensibiles divi­ tias de labore et periculis maris colligunt, quando multa lucrantur, tunc plura desiderant, et quæ ha­ bent, velut nihilum reputant; ad ea vero quae nec- dum habent omnem intentionem animi tendunt. Nos autem et eorum quae quaerenda sunt, nihil habemus, et nolumus possidere quæ necessaria sunt propter timorem Dei.
opinions.work: Verba Seniorum (Latin systematic Sayings of the Desert Fathers, tr. Pelagius the Deacon, 6th century)
opinions.location: book 5, 10.70 (On discretion); the last sentence is ambiguous in the Latin
opinions.translation: Own close rendering from the Latin Verba Seniorum of Pelagius the Deacon (Vitae Patrum book 5, PL 73), OCR text from Open Greek and Latin
opinions.today: Most people agree greed is endless. Fairly one-sided.

opinions.topic: new: staying put or moving on
opinions.position: Stay where you are. A monk or nun who keeps moving grows cold, like eggs abandoned by a hen.
opinions.side_note: Stability over restlessness.
opinions.quote: If you live in a monastery with others, do not change your place, for it will harm you. A hen that leaves the eggs she was warming makes them come out without chicks. So a monk or a virgin grows cold and dies in faith by passing from place to place.
opinions.original_latin: Si in monasterio cum aliis versaris, non mater locum ; laederis enim, si facias hoc. Etenim sicut gallina si dereliquerit ova sua fota, sine pullis ea exire facit ; ita mona­ chus vel virgo frigescit et mortificatur in fide, de loco ad locum transeundo.
opinions.work: Verba Seniorum (Latin systematic Sayings of the Desert Fathers, tr. Pelagius the Deacon, 6th century)
opinions.location: book 5, 7.18 (On patience); the Latin OCR reads "mater" for "mutes"
opinions.translation: Own close rendering from the Latin Verba Seniorum of Pelagius the Deacon (Vitae Patrum book 5, PL 73), OCR text from Open Greek and Latin
opinions.today: Strongly split. Modern culture prizes moving on for growth; others value staying and committing. Good quiz material.

opinions.position: Hide your good deeds. Praise melts the soul like wax and a known virtue is quickly spent.
opinions.side_note: Against doing good in public view.
opinions.quote: A treasure that is exposed is quickly spent; so any virtue, once it is known or made public, is destroyed. As wax melts before fire, so the soul is emptied by praise and loses the firmness of its virtues.
opinions.original_latin: Sicut thesaurus ma-, nifestus cito expenditur, ita et virtus quaelibet, cum innotuerit vel publicata fuerit, exterminabitur (Ruff., I. III, n. 114). Sicut enim cera solvitur a facie ignis, ita et anima laudibus inanitur; et amittit virtutum rigorem.
opinions.work: Verba Seniorum (Latin systematic Sayings of the Desert Fathers, tr. Pelagius the Deacon, 6th century)
opinions.location: book 5, 8.19 (That nothing should be done for show)
opinions.translation: Own close rendering from the Latin Verba Seniorum of Pelagius the Deacon (Vitae Patrum book 5, PL 73), OCR text from Open Greek and Latin
opinions.today: Split. Social media rewards visible good works; many still think they should be hidden (Matthew 6). Good quiz material.

opinions.position: Illness is not a disaster. Rejoice that God has visited you: fire takes rust off iron and proves gold.
opinions.side_note: A positive reading of suffering.
opinions.quote: Even if your body is cut down, burns with fever and is tormented by thirst, rejoice, because God has visited you. If you are iron, the fire will take off your rust. If you are righteous and suffer this, you move from great things to greater. You are gold, but through the fire you will be proven better.
opinions.original_latin: Sed quamvis concidatur corpus, et febribus validis inflammetur, insuper etiam intolerabili siti affligatur, si quidem peccator es qui haec sustines, re­ cordare futuri saeculi poenas, et aeternum ignem, et judicialia tormenta; et ita non deficies ad ea quae in praesenti contingunt; insuper et gaude, quia visita­ vit te Deus. Et illud famosissimum dictum in lingua habeto, id est, Castigans castigavit me Dominus, et morti non tradidit me (Psal. cxvii). Si ferrum es, per adhibitum tibi ignem amittes aeruginem.Quodsi justus es et haec pateris, de magno ad majora pro­ moveris. Aurum es, sed per ignem probatior eris.
opinions.work: Verba Seniorum (Latin systematic Sayings of the Desert Fathers, tr. Pelagius the Deacon, 6th century)
opinions.location: book 5, 7.19 (On patience); passage shortened in the English
opinions.translation: Own close rendering from the Latin Verba Seniorum of Pelagius the Deacon (Vitae Patrum book 5, PL 73), OCR text from Open Greek and Latin
opinions.today: Strongly split. Many find this comforting; many find it cruel to the sick. Handle with care.

opinions.position: Do not envy rich people's fine food. Fasting and plain fare beat their pleasures; do not even fill up on bread or long for wine.
opinions.side_note: Enjoyment: against food as pleasure.
opinions.quote: Do not let the delights of this world's rich seduce you, as if they held anything useful. They honour the art of seasoning food in many ways, for pleasure. You, by fasting and plain food, go beyond their abundance of delights. Do not even fill yourself with bread, nor long for wine.
opinions.original_latin: Non te seducant divitum hujus saeculi deliciae, tanquam utile aliquid habentes in se. Etenim illi delectationis causa artem diverso modo condiendi cibos honorant: tu autem jejunio et abje­ ctione ciborum abundantiam deliciarum illorum supergredere ; sed nec satielis pane, nec desideres vinum.
opinions.work: Verba Seniorum (Latin systematic Sayings of the Desert Fathers, tr. Pelagius the Deacon, 6th century)
opinions.translation: Own close rendering from the Latin Verba Seniorum of Pelagius the Deacon (Vitae Patrum book 5, PL 73), OCR text from Open Greek and Latin
opinions.today: Most people today enjoy good food without guilt. Strongly one-sided against her; useful as sparring material.

opinions.position: Loud, unrestrained laughter and roaming eyes go with folly, even in people who keep outward chastity.
opinions.side_note: Suspicious of unrestrained laughter.
opinions.quote: Among worldly people chastity also seems to be kept. But folly goes along with it, and through it they sin with all their other senses: they look where they should not and laugh without restraint.
opinions.original_latin: Etenim apud saecu­ lares videtur castitas observari: sed adest ei et stul­ titia, propter quam aliis omnibus sensibus peccant; nam et aspiciunt indecenter, et rident inordinate.
opinions.work: Verba Seniorum (Latin systematic Sayings of the Desert Fathers, tr. Pelagius the Deacon, 6th century)
opinions.translation: Own close rendering from the Latin Verba Seniorum of Pelagius the Deacon (Vitae Patrum book 5, PL 73), OCR text from Open Greek and Latin
opinions.today: Most people today see laughter as healthy. One-sided against her, but it pairs well with a question on seriousness.

opinions.position: Religious people can sink through complacency while worldly people, frightened by their storms, cry out to God and are saved.
opinions.side_note: A warning against feeling safe because you are devout.
opinions.quote: Often it happens that worldly people, sailing in storm and darkness, save their ship by crying out to God and keeping watch out of fear. We, in the calm, sink through that very neglect, while we let go of the rudder of justice.
opinions.original_latin: plerumque contingit ut saeculares illi in tempe­ state et in obscuro navigantes, pro metu periculi ad Deum clamando et vigilando salvent navim suam, nos autem in tranquillitate neglectu ipso demergi­ mur, dum gubernacula justitiae derelinquimus.
opinions.work: Verba Seniorum (Latin systematic Sayings of the Desert Fathers, tr. Pelagius the Deacon, 6th century)
opinions.translation: Own close rendering from the Latin Verba Seniorum of Pelagius the Deacon (Vitae Patrum book 5, PL 73), OCR text from Open Greek and Latin
opinions.today: Many people agree the devout can be complacent. Churchgoers may resist it. Good quiz material.

opinions.position: Turning to God is hard work and tears at first, then joy beyond words, like lighting a fire through the smoke.
opinions.side_note: Grace and effort: stresses effort and struggle.
opinions.quote: Those who turn to God face labour and a great struggle at first, and afterwards joy beyond words. People who want to light a fire are first choked by smoke and weep from it, and so they get what they want. So we too must kindle the divine fire in ourselves with tears and labour.
opinions.original_latin: Labor est et magnum certamen impiorum qui convertuntur ad Deum, et postea inenarrabile gaudium. Sicut enim qui ignem accendere volunt, prius fumantur, et ex fumi molestia lacrymantur, sicque obtinent quod vo­ lunt. Etenim scriptum est : Quia Deus noster igni s consumens est: ita oportet et |nos divinum ignem cum lacrymis atque laboribus in nobis ipsis accendere.
opinions.work: Verba Seniorum (Latin systematic Sayings of the Desert Fathers, tr. Pelagius the Deacon, 6th century)
opinions.translation: Own close rendering from the Latin Verba Seniorum of Pelagius the Deacon (Vitae Patrum book 5, PL 73), OCR text from Open Greek and Latin
opinions.today: Split. Many expect faith to feel good at once; others expect a hard start. Good quiz material.

opinions.position: No one can be saved without humility, as no ship can be built without nails.
opinions.side_note: Humility as essential.
opinions.quote: Just as a ship cannot be built without nails, so no one can be saved without humility.
opinions.original_latin: Dixit beatæ memoriae Syncletica : Sicut impos­ sibile est navim fabricari sine acutis, ita impossi­ bile est hominem sine humilitate salvari.
opinions.work: Verba Seniorum (Latin systematic Sayings of the Desert Fathers, tr. Pelagius the Deacon, 6th century)
opinions.translation: Own close rendering from the Latin Verba Seniorum of Pelagius the Deacon (Vitae Patrum book 5, PL 73), OCR text from Open Greek and Latin
opinions.today: Most agree in principle. One-sided.

sparring.with: No recorded clash with a named Christian
sparring.over: Her Life and sayings record no quarrels. Her implied opponents are ascetics who fast without measure, which puts her at odds with the harsher practice praised in the Life of Antony.
sparring.source: Verba Seniorum 10.72; Athanasius, Life of Antony 7 and 47

figures.name: Moses the Black
figures.dates: c. 330 to c. 405 (killed in a raid on Scetis; Palladius says he died at 75)
figures.places: Egypt; the monastic settlement of Scetis (Wadi el-Natrun)
figures.role: Former slave and robber-gang leader who became a monk, a priest at Scetis, and teacher of about seventy disciples
figures.status_note: Saint in the Coptic Orthodox Church (24 Paoni), Eastern Orthodox and Catholic Churches (28 August). Died a martyr in a barbarian raid on Scetis. Cautions: (1) "Ethiopian" in Greek usage meant a Black African, not necessarily someone from modern Ethiopia. (2) The Abbot Moses of Scete who speaks in Cassian's Conferences 1-2 is often identified with him, but this is not certain; Cassian also mentions an Abbot Moses of Calamus who fled to a monastery after a murder (Conference 3.5). Opinions taken from Cassian are marked. (3) Several stories involve racial insults from fellow monks; present them with care.
figures.hook: A slave thrown out for theft and violence, he became a gang leader who swam the flooded Nile with a sword in his teeth, then a monk so strong he carried four burglars to church on his back, and he died refusing to run from raiders.

stories.story: As a gang leader he wanted to kill a shepherd whose dogs had spoiled a raid. He swam the Nile in flood with his sword in his mouth. The shepherd hid in the sand, so Moses killed four rams, swam back with them, ate the best meat, and sold the skins for wine.
stories.source: Palladius, Lausiac History 19.1-3

stories.story: Four robbers broke into his cell. He tied them up, carried them on his back to the church, and asked the brothers what to do with them, since he was no longer allowed to hurt anyone. The robbers became monks.
stories.source: Palladius, Lausiac History 19.4; Sozomen, Church History 6.29

stories.story: Tormented for years by lust, he tried fasting, then standing all night for six years. Then he went out at night and secretly filled the water jars of the old monks, who fetched water from miles away. His teacher Isidore finally told him to stop fighting and come to Communion.
stories.source: Palladius, Lausiac History 19.5-10

stories.story: A council met at Scetis to judge a brother. Moses refused to come, then arrived carrying a leaking basket of sand. "My sins run out behind me and I cannot see them," he said, "and I have come to judge someone else." They forgave the brother.
stories.source: Budge, The Paradise vol. 2, Book I, ch. 10, no. 542

stories.story: To test him, the archbishop told the clergy to throw him out of the sanctuary with the words "Get outside, O Ethiopian." He went out telling himself they had treated him rightly.
stories.source: Budge, The Paradise vol. 2, Book I, ch. 10, no. 477

stories.story: When raiders came to Scetis he told the brothers to flee but stayed himself, saying he had waited years for the Lord's word "those who take the sword shall perish by the sword" to be fulfilled in him. Seven stayed with him and were killed.
stories.source: Budge, The Paradise vol. 2, Questions and Answers on the Rule of Life, no. 45

stories.story: Out of water with guests to feed, he paced in and out praying until rain filled every jar. Asked why he paced, he said he had been arguing his case with God.
stories.source: Budge, The Paradise vol. 2, Book I, ch. 13, no. 619

stories.story: A visitor was received coldly by the aristocratic Arsenius and warmly fed by Moses, and said he preferred "the Egyptian". An old monk then saw a vision of two boats: Arsenius sailing in silence with the Spirit of God, and Moses with angels feeding him honey.
stories.source: Budge, The Paradise vol. 2, Book I, ch. 1, nos. 21-22

temperament.evidence: Told by Isidore to stop battling his demons, he answered: "I will never cease until the appearance of the demons ceases."
temperament.source: Palladius, Lausiac History 19.10

temperament.evidence: Carried four bound robbers on his back "like a truss of straw".
temperament.source: Palladius, Lausiac History 19.4

temperament.trait: silent under insult, honest about fear
temperament.evidence: Monks sneered, "Why doth this Ethiopian come and go in our midst?" He said nothing, and afterwards admitted: "Although I was afraid I uttered not a word."
temperament.source: Budge, The Paradise vol. 2, Book I, ch. 1, no. 55

temperament.evidence: He cooked for visiting brothers during a fast week; the clergy said he broke men's rule but kept God's.
temperament.source: Budge, The Paradise vol. 2, Book I, ch. 9, no. 441

temperament.evidence: He "entered into judgement with God" when he had no water for guests.
temperament.source: Budge, The Paradise vol. 2, Book I, ch. 13, no. 619

misattributed.line: The judging story told with "a leaking jug of water"
misattributed.truth: Not a fake: the Greek alphabetical collection has a leaking jug; the Syriac collection translated by Budge has a basket of sand. Name the version you quote.

misattributed.line: Teachings on discretion and "purity of heart" quoted as Moses the Black's
misattributed.truth: These come from Cassian's Conferences 1-2, whose Abbot Moses of Scete may or may not be Moses the Black. Label them "Abba Moses in Cassian".

opinions.position: Do not sit in judgment on a sinner. Look at your own sins first; you cannot even see them all.
opinions.side_note: Correction: firmly against condemning.
opinions.quote: my sins which are running down behind me and I cannot see them, and I, even I, have come this day to judge shortcomings which are not mine.
opinions.work: Sayings of the Desert Fathers (Syriac collection, in Budge, The Paradise, vol. 2)
opinions.translation: E. A. Wallis Budge, The Paradise or Garden of the Holy Fathers, vol. 2 (1907), from the Syriac collection of ʿAnan-Isho; Wikisource transcription
opinions.today: Most agree in principle. Many also believe in holding people accountable, so it can still split.

opinions.position: Mourn your own dead, not your neighbour's. If you look closely at your own sins you will not see your neighbour's.
opinions.side_note: Correction: self-examination before any judgment.
opinions.quote: If we allow ourselves to view closely our own sins we shall not see those of our neighbour. It is folly for a man to forsake his own dead and to lament over that of his neighbour.
opinions.work: Sayings of the Desert Fathers (Syriac collection, in Budge, The Paradise, vol. 2)
opinions.location: Book II, Questions and Answers on the Rule of Life, no. 126
opinions.translation: E. A. Wallis Budge, The Paradise or Garden of the Holy Fathers, vol. 2 (1907), from the Syriac collection of ʿAnan-Isho; Wikisource transcription
opinions.today: Most agree in principle.

opinions.position: Do not resist violent attackers with force. He stayed to die, citing "Those who take the sword shall perish by the sword" about himself, but left others free to flee.
opinions.side_note: War: for non-resistance, applied to himself, not imposed on others.
opinions.quote: I have been expecting this day to come for many years past, so that might be fulfilled the command of our Redeemer, Who said, ‘Those who take the sword shall perish by the sword’
opinions.work: Sayings of the Desert Fathers (Syriac collection, in Budge, The Paradise, vol. 2)
opinions.location: Book II, Questions and Answers on the Rule of Life, no. 45
opinions.translation: E. A. Wallis Budge, The Paradise or Garden of the Holy Fathers, vol. 2 (1907), from the Syriac collection of ʿAnan-Isho; Wikisource transcription
opinions.today: Strongly split. Most people think self-defence is right; pacifists and many who admire him disagree. Good quiz material.

opinions.position: Whether to flee danger is each person's own choice. He told the brothers to run, and when they insisted on staying, said it was their decision, not his.
opinions.side_note: Flight: permits flight; will not command martyrdom.
opinions.quote: This is not my affair, but your own desire; let every man look after himself in the place where he dwelleth.
opinions.work: Sayings of the Desert Fathers (Syriac collection, in Budge, The Paradise, vol. 2)
opinions.location: Book II, Questions and Answers on the Rule of Life, no. 45
opinions.translation: E. A. Wallis Budge, The Paradise or Garden of the Holy Fathers, vol. 2 (1907), from the Syriac collection of ʿAnan-Isho; Wikisource transcription
opinions.today: Most people today would say fleeing is right. His respect for each person's choice is widely shared.

opinions.position: A Christian may stop wrongdoers but must not harm them; he handed the burglars he had overpowered to the church instead of punishing them.
opinions.side_note: Restraint without revenge.
opinions.quote: Since I am not allowed to hurt anyone, what do you bid me do with these?
opinions.work: Palladius, Lausiac History
opinions.translation: W. K. Lowther Clarke, The Lausiac History of Palladius (1918), transcribed by Roger Pearse
opinions.today: Split. Most would restrain a burglar and call the police; few would refuse to press charges. Good quiz material.

opinions.position: No past is too dark. A robber and killer became a priest and a saint, and his conversion led the robbers he caught to convert too.
opinions.side_note: Second chances: his life is the argument (the words here are the robbers').
opinions.quote: If he who was so great and powerful in brigandage has feared God, why should we defer our salvation?
opinions.work: Palladius, Lausiac History
opinions.translation: W. K. Lowther Clarke, The Lausiac History of Palladius (1918), transcribed by Roger Pearse
opinions.today: Most people say they believe in second chances; far fewer would trust a former killer as a leader. Split in practice.

opinions.position: Stay in your cell; it will teach you everything. The one who flees the world ripens; the one who stays among people stays sour.
opinions.side_note: Solitude: strongly for withdrawal (yet he was famous for welcoming guests).
opinions.quote: The man who fleeth from the world is like unto ripe grapes, but he who dwelleth among the attractions of the children of men is like unto sour grapes.
opinions.work: Sayings of the Desert Fathers (Syriac collection, in Budge, The Paradise, vol. 2)
opinions.translation: E. A. Wallis Budge, The Paradise or Garden of the Holy Fathers, vol. 2 (1907), from the Syriac collection of ʿAnan-Isho; Wikisource transcription
opinions.today: Most people think we grow among others. Split.

opinions.position: Welcoming guests can outrank a religious rule. He cooked for visitors during a fast week, and the clergy defended him.
opinions.side_note: Mercy over rule-keeping (his action; the verdict is the clergy's).
opinions.quote: O Abbâ Moses, though thou dost break the command of men, thou stablishest [that of God].
opinions.work: Sayings of the Desert Fathers (Syriac collection, in Budge, The Paradise, vol. 2)
opinions.location: Book I, chapter 9, no. 441 (the clergy speaking)
opinions.translation: E. A. Wallis Budge, The Paradise or Garden of the Holy Fathers, vol. 2 (1907), from the Syriac collection of ʿAnan-Isho; Wikisource transcription
opinions.today: Most people agree that kindness beats rules. Some traditional believers would disagree about breaking a fast.

opinions.position: When insulted for his colour he kept silent and even told himself the insult was deserved.
opinions.side_note: Accepting humiliation without retaliation.
opinions.quote: They have treated thee rightly, O thou whose skin is dark and black; thou shalt not go back as if thou wert a [white] man.
opinions.work: Sayings of the Desert Fathers (Syriac collection, in Budge, The Paradise, vol. 2)
opinions.translation: E. A. Wallis Budge, The Paradise or Garden of the Holy Fathers, vol. 2 (1907), from the Syriac collection of ʿAnan-Isho; Wikisource transcription
opinions.today: Strongly split and sensitive. Many today would call this internalised racism and urge speaking up; others see radical humility. Use with great care, if at all.

opinions.position: Prayer must be matched by deeds, or it is wasted.
opinions.side_note: Grace and effort: prayer and effort together.
opinions.quote: If works do not correspond to prayer he who prayeth laboureth in vain.
opinions.work: Sayings of the Desert Fathers (Syriac collection, in Budge, The Paradise, vol. 2)
opinions.location: Book II, Questions and Answers on the Rule of Life, no. 123
opinions.translation: E. A. Wallis Budge, The Paradise or Garden of the Holy Fathers, vol. 2 (1907), from the Syriac collection of ʿAnan-Isho; Wikisource transcription
opinions.today: Most agree. One-sided.

opinions.topic: new: seeing yourself as a sinner
opinions.position: Only someone who stands before God as a sinner is heard in prayer.
opinions.side_note: Humility in prayer.
opinions.quote: If a man doth not put himself in the attitude of a sinner, his prayer will not be heard before God.
opinions.work: Sayings of the Desert Fathers (Syriac collection, in Budge, The Paradise, vol. 2)
opinions.location: Book II, Questions and Answers on the Rule of Life, no. 122
opinions.translation: E. A. Wallis Budge, The Paradise or Garden of the Holy Fathers, vol. 2 (1907), from the Syriac collection of ʿAnan-Isho; Wikisource transcription
opinions.today: Split. Many modern believers stress self-worth; traditional believers stress confessing sin.

opinions.position: It is right to press your case with God when others are in need.
opinions.side_note: Bold, complaining prayer.
opinions.quote: I entered into judgement with God, who brought me hither because there was want of water, and because I had no water for His servants to drink
opinions.work: Sayings of the Desert Fathers (Syriac collection, in Budge, The Paradise, vol. 2)
opinions.translation: E. A. Wallis Budge, The Paradise or Garden of the Holy Fathers, vol. 2 (1907), from the Syriac collection of ʿAnan-Isho; Wikisource transcription
opinions.today: Split. Some think arguing with God is irreverent; others think it is honest faith (as in the Psalms and Job).

opinions.position: Too much fasting and too little sleep do more harm than overeating, because the cure for overeating is easy and the cure for excess is not. (Abba Moses in Cassian; identity uncertain.)
opinions.side_note: Asceticism: moderation; excess worse than laxity.
opinions.quote: excessive abstinence is still more injurious to us than careless satiety
opinions.work: John Cassian, Conferences (Abbot Moses speaking)
opinions.translation: E. C. S. Gibson, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, vol. 11 (1894), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Most people agree today. Among the desert Fathers it was a live dispute.

opinions.position: Never crush someone who confesses a struggle; comfort them. (Abba Moses in Cassian, telling of an elder who harshly rebuked a young monk and was then tempted himself.)
opinions.side_note: Correction: gentle, against shaming.
opinions.quote: never to terrify with destructive despair those who are in danger, nor harden them with severe speeches, but rather restore them with gentle and kindly consolations
opinions.work: John Cassian, Conferences (Abbot Moses speaking)
opinions.translation: E. C. S. Gibson, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, vol. 11 (1894), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Most agree today. One-sided.

opinions.topic: new: telling someone your secret struggles
opinions.position: Tell your hidden thoughts to a wise elder. Evil thoughts rule only while they stay hidden. (Abba Moses in Cassian.)
opinions.side_note: For confession and spiritual direction.
opinions.quote: For evil thoughts will hold sway in us just so long as they are hidden in the heart
opinions.work: John Cassian, Conferences (Abbot Moses speaking)
opinions.translation: E. C. S. Gibson, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, vol. 11 (1894), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split. Therapy culture agrees strongly; many people prefer privacy, and many Protestants reject confession to a person.

opinions.position: Grey hair alone earns no authority. Follow only elders whose lives proved them. (Abba Moses in Cassian.)
opinions.side_note: Against deference to age as such.
opinions.quote: For the true riches of old men are not to be measured by grey hairs but by their diligence in youth and the rewards of their past labours.
opinions.work: John Cassian, Conferences (Abbot Moses speaking)
opinions.translation: E. C. S. Gibson, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, vol. 11 (1894), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Most people today agree. One-sided.

sparring.over: His colour. Monks sneered "Why doth this Ethiopian come and go in our midst?" and the clergy, on the archbishop's orders, drove him out of the sanctuary as a test.
sparring.source: Budge, The Paradise vol. 2, Book I, ch. 1, no. 55 and ch. 10, no. 477

sparring.over: Isidore told him to stop provoking the demons; Moses refused until his dreams ended.

sparring.source: Budge, The Paradise vol. 2, Book I, ch. 1, nos. 21-22

figures.name: Arsenius the Great
figures.dates: c. 354 to c. 449 (Budge's source says he died at 95)
figures.places: Rome; the imperial court at Constantinople; Scetis; Troe near Memphis; Canopus near Alexandria
figures.role: Roman aristocrat and tutor at the court of Theodosius I (to his sons Arcadius and Honorius, by tradition) who fled to the Egyptian desert and became its most silent monk
figures.status_note: Saint in the Eastern Orthodox Church (8 May), Coptic Church, and Catholic Church (19 July). Caution: the court details (tutor to the princes, a thousand slaves) come from the sayings and later tradition; the sayings are near-contemporary but not checked against court records.
figures.hook: Once the most finely dressed man at the imperial court, he fled to the desert, sat behind a pillar in church so no one could see his face, and wept until his eyelashes wore away.

stories.story: At court he prayed "Lord, direct me how to live" and heard: "Arsenius, flee from men, and thou shalt live."
stories.source: Budge, The Paradise vol. 2, Book I, ch. 1, no. 1

stories.story: A noble Roman woman sailed to Egypt to see him. He scolded her for coming and, when she asked him to remember her in prayer, said he would pray God to wipe her memory from his heart. She fell ill with grief until the archbishop explained.
stories.source: Budge, The Paradise vol. 2, Book I, ch. 8, no. 253

stories.story: An old monk was offended to see him sick on a mat with a pillow. The priest pointed out that the old monk had been a poor shepherd and now lived better than ever, while Arsenius had given up a palace.
stories.source: Budge, The Paradise vol. 2, Book I, ch. 10, no. 450

stories.story: A lawyer brought him a relative's will leaving him a fortune. He went to tear it up, saying he had died before his relative.
stories.source: Budge, The Paradise vol. 2, Questions and Answers on the Rule of Life, no. 517

temperament.evidence: He sat behind a pillar in church so no one would see his face, and his eyelashes were worn away by weeping.
temperament.source: Budge, The Paradise vol. 2, Book I, ch. 5, no. 165

temperament.evidence: Asked by Archbishop Theophilus for a word, he said: "In whatsoever place ye hear that Arsenius is, come not nigh thereunto."
temperament.source: Budge, The Paradise vol. 2, Book I, ch. 1, no. 52

temperament.evidence: He asked an Egyptian peasant about his thoughts, saying he knew Greek and Latin but not "the alphabet of this villager".
temperament.source: Budge, The Paradise vol. 2, Questions and Answers on the Rule of Life, no. 234

misattributed.line: "I have often regretted speaking, but never regretted keeping silent"
misattributed.truth: Genuinely in his sayings, but it is an older classical proverb: Plutarch gives it to the poet Simonides, and Valerius Maximus to Xenocrates. Arsenius used an existing proverb. Secondary knowledge, not re-read here.

opinions.position: He loved people but could not be with God and with men at once, so he chose God and fled them.
opinions.side_note: Solitude: the extreme of withdrawal.
opinions.quote: God knoweth that I love you, but I cannot be both with God and with men.
opinions.work: Sayings of the Desert Fathers (Syriac collection, in Budge, The Paradise, vol. 2)
opinions.translation: E. A. Wallis Budge, The Paradise or Garden of the Holy Fathers, vol. 2 (1907), from the Syriac collection of ʿAnan-Isho; Wikisource transcription
opinions.today: Most people today think God is found with others. Strongly split.

opinions.position: Speech is often regretted, silence never.
opinions.side_note: Silence: strongly for it.
opinions.quote: I have many times repented that I spoke, but that I held my peace I have never repented.
opinions.work: Sayings of the Desert Fathers (Syriac collection, in Budge, The Paradise, vol. 2)
opinions.translation: E. A. Wallis Budge, The Paradise or Garden of the Holy Fathers, vol. 2 (1907), from the Syriac collection of ʿAnan-Isho; Wikisource transcription
opinions.today: Many agree; talkers and people who value speaking up for others disagree.

opinions.position: An uneducated peasant's spiritual wisdom is worth more than Greek and Latin learning.
opinions.side_note: Learning: humbles book learning before lived wisdom.
opinions.quote: With Greek and Latin learning I am well acquainted, but I have not yet learned the alphabet of this villager.
opinions.work: Sayings of the Desert Fathers (Syriac collection, in Budge, The Paradise, vol. 2)
opinions.location: Book II, Questions and Answers on the Rule of Life, no. 234
opinions.translation: E. A. Wallis Budge, The Paradise or Garden of the Holy Fathers, vol. 2 (1907), from the Syriac collection of ʿAnan-Isho; Wikisource transcription
opinions.today: Many agree; academics and many believers value formal study more.

opinions.position: He refused a large inheritance, saying he was already dead to the world.
opinions.side_note: Wealth: complete renunciation.
opinions.quote: I died before he did, though he hath only now died, but shall I live?
opinions.work: Sayings of the Desert Fathers (Syriac collection, in Budge, The Paradise, vol. 2)
opinions.location: Book II, Questions and Answers on the Rule of Life, no. 517
opinions.translation: E. A. Wallis Budge, The Paradise or Garden of the Holy Fathers, vol. 2 (1907), from the Syriac collection of ʿAnan-Isho; Wikisource transcription
opinions.today: Few people today would refuse an inheritance. Strongly one-sided against him.

opinions.position: Denying yourself every small pleasure is good, but each person must do what he can; if you cannot, plant the herbs again.
opinions.side_note: Enjoyment: strict ideal, lenient allowance.
opinions.quote: This is good, but every man [must do] as he is able, and if he hath not strength to persist in this perhaps he should plant others.
opinions.work: Sayings of the Desert Fathers (Syriac collection, in Budge, The Paradise, vol. 2)
opinions.location: Book II, Questions and Answers on the Rule of Life, no. 397
opinions.translation: E. A. Wallis Budge, The Paradise or Garden of the Holy Fathers, vol. 2 (1907), from the Syriac collection of ʿAnan-Isho; Wikisource transcription
opinions.today: Most people would side with his leniency.

opinions.topic: new: friendship between men and women
opinions.position: He did not want a woman visitor's memory in his heart and scolded her for travelling to see him.
opinions.side_note: Keeping away from the other sex.
opinions.quote: I will pray to God that He may blot out the memory of thee from my heart
opinions.work: Sayings of the Desert Fathers (Syriac collection, in Budge, The Paradise, vol. 2)
opinions.translation: E. A. Wallis Budge, The Paradise or Garden of the Holy Fathers, vol. 2 (1907), from the Syriac collection of ʿAnan-Isho; Wikisource transcription
opinions.today: Most people today find this harsh and sexist. Strongly one-sided against him; use only as a sparring point.

opinions.position: Even a holy man should fear the hour of death; he wept as he died.
opinions.side_note: Fear of death as lifelong companion.
opinions.quote: The dread of this hour hath been with me in very truth from the time when I became a monk, and was afraid.
opinions.work: Sayings of the Desert Fathers (Syriac collection, in Budge, The Paradise, vol. 2)
opinions.translation: E. A. Wallis Budge, The Paradise or Garden of the Holy Fathers, vol. 2 (1907), from the Syriac collection of ʿAnan-Isho; Wikisource transcription
opinions.today: Split. Some Christians say believers should not fear death; others find his honesty right.

opinions.position: One hour of sleep is enough for a committed monk.
opinions.side_note: Asceticism: severe on sleep.
opinions.quote: One hour’s sleep is sufficient for a monk, provided that he be strenuous.
opinions.work: Sayings of the Desert Fathers (Syriac collection, in Budge, The Paradise, vol. 2)
opinions.translation: E. A. Wallis Budge, The Paradise or Garden of the Holy Fathers, vol. 2 (1907), from the Syriac collection of ʿAnan-Isho; Wikisource transcription
opinions.today: Almost everyone today would call this unhealthy. One-sided against him.

sparring.source: Budge, The Paradise vol. 2, Book I, ch. 1, no. 52

sparring.over: "Why fleest thou from us?" Arsenius: he could not be with God and men both.
sparring.source: Budge, The Paradise vol. 2, Book I, ch. 1, no. 53

sparring.over: Arsenius's pillow and mat when sick; the priest defended Arsenius.

figures.name: Poemen the Great
figures.places: Scetis; after the raids of 407, Terenuthis and other places in lower Egypt
figures.role: Desert monk, leader of a band of brothers (including his own brothers Job and Paesius); the most-quoted voice in the Sayings of the Desert Fathers
figures.status_note: Saint in the Eastern Orthodox Church (27 August), the Coptic Church and the Catholic Church. Caution: "Poemen" (shepherd) may have been a name used by more than one monk, and some sayings under his name may belong to others. The Syriac collection (Budge) sometimes marks doubt, e.g. "Abbâ Poemen (or Ammon)".
figures.hook: Told that monks should wake brothers who doze in church, he said he puts the sleeper's head on his knees and lets him rest.

stories.story: Old monks asked whether to hit brothers who fell asleep during the service. He said he would rest the sleeper's head on his knees.
stories.source: Budge, The Paradise vol. 2, Book I, ch. 9, no. 443

stories.story: A judge jailed Poemen's nephew to force him to visit. His sister wept and cursed him at his door. He sent word, "Poemen hath no sons", and told the judge to try the case by law.
stories.source: Budge, The Paradise vol. 2, Book I, ch. 8, no. 265

stories.story: Abba Isaac caught him washing his feet and asked how he could, when the old Fathers were so harsh on their bodies. He said monks learn to kill passions, not bodies.
stories.source: Budge, The Paradise vol. 2, Questions and Answers on the Rule of Life, no. 166

stories.story: Heretics came and slandered the archbishop. He said nothing, had a table laid, fed them and sent them away in peace.
stories.source: Budge, The Paradise vol. 2, Book I, ch. 8, no. 284

stories.story: Told of a hermit who boasted he had not been into the village for years, Poemen said he would walk round the village at night so his thoughts could not boast.
stories.source: Budge, The Paradise vol. 2, Book I, ch. 8, no. 289

temperament.evidence: If he passed a brother sinning, "I should pass him by and not see him."
temperament.source: Budge, The Paradise vol. 2, Book I, ch. 8, no. 285

temperament.evidence: He sent visitors to his older brother Job, and "never wished to magnify his word over that of any old man".
temperament.source: Budge, The Paradise vol. 2, Questions and Answers on the Rule of Life, no. 350

temperament.evidence: Pressed to eat at an odd hour, he would go "with the tears streaming from his eyes" rather than upset a brother.
temperament.source: Budge, The Paradise vol. 2, Book I, ch. 9, no. 411

temperament.evidence: He refused his own sister's pleas for her jailed son.
temperament.source: Budge, The Paradise vol. 2, Book I, ch. 8, no. 265
